strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine gap in test-time scaling—tree-search policies are budget-agnostic and treat the token budget merely as a termination condition—and articulates two concrete failure modes (late over-branching vs. premature termination).

The proposed method is simple, coherent, and well-specified: budget-conditioned PUCT (annealed exploration + depth-biased value correction) and a budget-gated widening trigger via a virtual generative child (Eqs. 3-7) are cleanly integrated into the standard MCTS loop, and Algorithm 1 plus the appendices make the method reproducible in principle.

Comprehensive empirical protocol: 2 models x 2 benchmarks (MATH500 Lv.5, AIME24/25) x 3 budgets, with sensible baselines (repeated sampling, sequential refinement, MCTS, AB-MCTS-M, LiteSearch), an honest budget-consumption definition for early-stopping baselines (Appendix C), a component ablation (Table 2), and multiple mechanistic analyses (answer-reach rate, depth/width trajectories, node precision, qualitative tree visualizations) that directly support the claimed wide-to-deep behavior.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper transparently explains why AB-MCTS-M underperforms in its setting, acknowledges the sparse reward landscape of GenPRM-7B, notes the lower answer-reach rate and reduced coverage, and flags reward-model cost as unaccounted future work.
weaknesses: The headline gains are modest and sometimes marginal: in several settings BG-MCTS ties or only slightly exceeds strong baselines (e.g., Llama MATH500 10K: .393 vs. .393 for Repeated; Qwen AIME 10K: .156 vs. .156 for MCTS/Repeated; Qwen AIME 30K: .183 vs. .183 for Repeated), and differences like .465 vs. .438 are reported over only three trials with no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so the 'consistently outperforms' claim is weakly supported statistically.

The budget accounting is incomplete in a way that likely favors tree-search methods: Cused counts only policy-LLM output tokens, while every node expansion invokes a generative reward model (GenPRM-7B) whose own generated reasoning tokens can be substantial. Tree search invokes the RM far more often than repeated sampling per unit of policy tokens, so the reported fixed-budget comparisons do not reflect true inference cost; the paper defers this to future work without quantifying the effect.

The method is a collection of heuristic modifications to PUCT (multiplicative ρ on exploration, additive depth bias, ρ-scaled variance bonus for widening) with fixed hyperparameters (κ = λ = 1) and no sensitivity analysis; it is unclear how robust the design is across reward models, model scales, or domains beyond math, especially given the authors' own observation that the reward signal is near-binary and weakly discriminative.

The ablation results are noisy and partially undercut the complementarity claim: full BG-MCTS is not always the best configuration (e.g., Qwen 10K: .662 vs. .649 for exploration-annealing only; Qwen 30K: .711 vs. .720 for Explore+Widen; several ablations fall below the MCTS baseline, indicating high run-to-run variance), and the ablation uses only two runs.

Evaluated only on mathematical reasoning with sub-10B instruction-tuned models; the paper argues this is the realistic regime, but no evidence is given that budget conditioning helps stronger models or other task families, and the depth-based completion bias (Eq. 5) presupposes a predictable answer depth that may not generalize.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a method whose behavior depends on many implementation details (node construction, '
Step' delimiting, 'But wait' continuation prompting, reward-model chat template).

strengths: The problem framing is clear and practically motivated: existing tree-search decoding treats the token budget only as a stopping condition, and the paper articulates two concrete failure modes (late over-branching vs. premature termination) that budget conditioning addresses.

The method is clearly specified and self-contained: BG-PUCT (Eq. 3), the depth-biased value correction (Eqs. 4-5), the virtual generative child with an uncertainty-driven widening score (Eq. 6), and the unified selection rule (Eq. 7) are all fully described, with Algorithm 1 summarizing the procedure.

The evaluation covers 12 settings (2 models x 2 benchmarks x 3 budgets) against several relevant tree-search baselines (MCTS, AB-MCTS-M, LiteSearch) plus parallel and sequential scaling baselines, and includes an ablation (Table 2) of all three components and a reasonable hyperparameter search (Appendix B).

The analysis goes beyond headline accuracy: answer-reach rate over consumed budget (Figs. 3, 8, 9), node-level precision statistics (Tables 3-4), depth/width trajectories (Figs. 4, 10, 11), and qualitative tree visualizations (Figs. 5, 12-15) collectively support the claimed wide-to-deep behavioral shift.

The discussion is candid about weaknesses of the current setup, particularly the near-binary reward landscape of GenPRM-7B, and acknowledges that input tokens and reward computation are excluded from the budget.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated relative to the evidence. BG-MCTS 'consistently outperforms budget-agnostic tree-search baselines', but the simple Repeated Sampling baseline often matches or beats it: on Llama MATH500 30K, Repeated (.450) exceeds BG-MCTS (.443); on Qwen AIME24/25 10K, they tie (.156); on Qwen MATH500 30K, Repeated (.702) is very close to BG-MCTS (.711). Gains over tree-search baselines are real but modest, and the strongest baseline is not beaten reliably, weakening the practical significance of the contribution.

Statistical support is thin. AIME24/25 has only 30 problems, and accuracies are averaged over three trials with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported anywhere. Many cell differences (e.g., .083 vs .089) are well within plausible noise, so 'best in 11 of 12 settings' is fragile.

The budget accounting is narrow in a way that may distort comparisons: only policy-model output tokens are counted, while the cost of GenPRM-7B verifier calls (which generate reasoning per node) and input tokens are excluded. Tree-search methods call the verifier far more often than Repeated Sampling/Refinement, so the effective compute gap may be much smaller than the reported token budget suggests; the paper defers this to future work but it directly affects the fairness of the fixed-budget protocol.

The method is a combination of hand-tuned heuristics with limited justification: kappa = lambda = 1 is fixed with no sensitivity analysis; the depth-bias term kappa(1-rho)d(x)/d_ans mixes a depth bonus into the value scale without theoretical grounding; and the ablation results are mixed (e.g., on Qwen 30K, Eq. 3 alone gives .720 vs. .711 for the full method), making it hard to attribute the improvements to the proposed components rather than hyperparameter luck.

Comparability concerns in baseline setup: different node-generation units (Full vs. Sequential) are used across baselines partly to 'match the original paper', greedy pre-generation is disabled in LiteSearch, and AB-MCTS-M performs far below expectations in this setting (.124-.209 on MATH500 with Llama), which the authors attribute to setting mismatch. These choices make head-to-head conclusions less reliable.

Scope is narrow: only two math benchmarks, two sub-10B instruction-tuned models, and a single reward model. Whether budget conditioning helps for other domains, stronger models, or better-calibrated reward models is untested, yet the abstract and conclusion imply generality.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, and some reproducibility details (exact reward-model call protocol, how d_ans is maintained per instance, variance of Q used in Eq. 6) require more precision than the appendix provides.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: existing tree-search decoding policies treat the token budget only as a termination condition, causing late-stage over-branching or premature termination. Framing budget-conditioned selection and widening is a sensible and reasonably novel angle.

The method is clearly presented: the three mechanisms (budget-annealed exploration in Eq. 3, depth-biased value correction in Eq. 5, and budget-guided widening in Eq. 6) are cleanly built on top of standard PUCT, and Algorithm 1 makes the procedure easy to follow.

The empirical study is reasonably thorough for the regime considered: 2 models, 2 benchmarks, 3 budgets, multiple tree-search and sampling baselines, a component ablation (Table 2), budget-profile analyses (Figs. 2–4), node-level precision statistics (Table 3), and qualitative tree visualizations that directly illustrate the intended wide-to-deep behavior.

Reproducibility support is decent: appendices detail the hyperparameter search for baselines, answer extraction rules, prompt templates for both the policy LLM and the reward model, and a careful description of how LiteSearch's early stopping is handled fairly in tables vs. graphs.

The discussion is honest: the authors acknowledge that AB-MCTS-M underperforms in their setting, that the reward model (GenPRM-7B) is nearly binary and weakly discriminative, that the lower answer-reach rate limits data-coverage use cases, and they correctly defer input-token and reward-compute accounting to future work.
weaknesses: Evidence for the headline claim is limited to a narrow regime: two math benchmarks, two sub-10B instruction-tuned models, one reward model, and output-token-only budget accounting. No experiments beyond mathematics or with larger/frontier models, so the generality of 'budget-aligned search is more effective' remains unverified outside this niche.

Gains over the strongest baseline are modest and inconsistent: on Math500, BG-MCTS roughly ties or slightly loses to Repeated Sampling in several cells (e.g., Llama 10K: .393 vs .393; 30K: .443 vs .450), and on Qwen AIME 10K (.156) it ties Repeated Sampling. The consistent advantage is only over the tree-search baselines, which themselves often underperform simple parallel sampling — raising questions about the practical significance of the contribution.

No statistical rigor: results are averaged over three trials (two for ablations) with no variance estimates or significance tests. AIME24/25 has only 30 problems per year, so differences like .156 vs .189 are well within plausible noise; this is not addressed.

The method is a stack of heuristics with several introduced constants (κ, λ, the exploration annealing schedule, the ˆd_ans estimate). κ = λ = 1 is chosen without justification or sensitivity analysis, and no theory supports the design; it is unclear how fragile the approach is to these choices, reward scale, or budget size.

Reward-model compute is excluded from the budget even though every expanded node requires an RM call, and tree-search methods typically issue many more RM calls per output token than Repeated Sampling; the cost accounting may therefore favor BG-MCTS relative to the sampling baselines.

The depth-bias term in Eq. 5 boosts Q-values of deeper nodes within a subtree via d(x)/ˆd_ans, which conflates 'depth' with 'completion promise' and could reward long low-quality branches; the paper does not analyze potential failure cases of this shaping.

No code release is mentioned, and the hyperparameters of BG-MCTS itself were apparently not tuned as carefully as those of the baselines (Appendix B tunes only MCTS's c and expansion width), leaving the exact configuration of the proposed method under-specified for reproduction.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem setting: fixed per-query token budgets are realistic for API/token-metered deployment, and the observation that existing tree-search policies treat the budget only as a stopping condition is a genuine and relatable gap.

The method is concrete and fully specified: BG-PUCT with ρ-annealed exploration (Eq. 3), depth-biased completion shaping (Eq. 5), and budget-guided widening via a virtual generative child (Eq. 6) are all described precisely, with an algorithm box that makes the method reproducible.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-32B), two math benchmarks plus an additional physics benchmark (UGPhysics), three budget levels, and multiple strong baselines (Repeated Sampling, Sequential Refinement, MCTS, AB-MCTS-M, LiteSearch, beam search).

Thoughtful analysis beyond headline accuracy: depth–width trade-off curves, answer-reach-rate trajectories, answered-node precision statistics (Table 11), qualitative tree visualizations, hyperparameter sensitivity (Appendix G), an honest discussion of PRM score saturation (Appendix K), and a careful accounting protocol for LiteSearch's early stopping (Appendix C).

Ablations (Table 2) support the claim that the three components are complementary rather than a single lucky heuristic, and the mechanism-level results (Figures 4, 6, 7) are consistent with the intended wide-to-deep behavior rather than being post-hoc rationalizations.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is fairly incremental: each component (multiplying the exploration bonus by a remaining-budget ratio, adding a depth-proportional bias, annealing widening) is a plausible hand-crafted heuristic rather than a principled solution; there is no theoretical or optimality-based justification for the specific functional forms or the choice of κ = λ = 1.

Margins over the strongest baselines are sometimes small and the 'consistently outperforms' claim is overstated: on MATH500 with Llama-3.1-8B, BG-MCTS loses to Repeated Sampling at 30K (.443 vs .450) and the average gap (.434 vs .427) is within what 3-trial noise could plausibly produce; no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere in the main results.

Some ablation cells are weak or contradictory (e.g., removing the widening annealing alone drops below the plain MCTS baseline in several cells, and Table 7 shows the no-generative-node variant beating full BG-MCTS at 10K), suggesting the full configuration is not uniformly superior and its components interact in ways not fully explained.

Baselines use different node-generation units (Sequential for tree search, Full for repeated sampling/AB-MCTS-M), which introduces a confound between the budget-aware policy and the node representation; the paper acknowledges this but does not isolate its effect.

The physics evaluation uses only 120 sampled questions with a rollout-based evaluator whose non-terminal scores are near zero, a regime the authors themselves show disadvantages score-based baselines (Appendix F.3), weakening the generality claim; several appendix comparisons are single-run.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which, combined with many implementation details relegated to appendices, limits reproducibility for a method with several interacting hyperparameters.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and well-motivated problem: making tree-search decoding policies aware of a fixed per-query token budget, rather than treating the budget purely as a stopping condition.

The proposed mechanisms (budget-annealed exploration in BG-PUCT, depth-biased value correction, budget-guided widening via a virtual generative child) are clearly specified, and Algorithm 1 plus appendices give enough implementation detail to follow the method.

The empirical evaluation is broad: three open-weight LLMs, MATH500/AIME24-25 plus a complementary physics benchmark (UGPhysics), multiple budgets, and multiple baselines (repeated sampling, sequential refinement, AB-MCTS-M, MCTS, LiteSearch, beam search).

The analysis goes beyond headline accuracy: depth/width trajectories, answered-node statistics, qualitative tree visualizations, an ablation of the three components, a hyperparameter sensitivity sweep, and an honest discussion of PRM score saturation (Appendix K) and its implications.
Limitations are discussed candidly (saturated reward signal, coverage/quality trade-off for data synthesis), which is appropriate treatment of weaknesses rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is incremental: multiplying the PUCT exploration bonus by the remaining-budget ratio ρ, adding a depth bias scaled by (1−ρ), and scaling a widening term by ρ are straightforward heuristic modifications of PUCT with no theoretical grounding or analysis of when such annealing should help. The completion-bias term (Eq. 5) could plausibly push selection toward deep-but-wrong branches, and no analysis addresses this risk.

Evidence for the central claim is noisier than the text suggests. In the ablation (Table 2), the full method is not consistently best per budget (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B at 30K: full .443 vs. an ablated variant at .485), and several single-component ablations improve over full BG-MCTS at specific budgets, which undercuts the claim that the three components are complementary. Results are 'averaged over three trials' but no standard deviations or significance tests are reported anywhere, so many of the margins in Tables 1 and 3 (often a few points) are hard to distinguish from run-to-run variance.

Gains over the strongest baselines are modest in absolute terms (e.g., Qwen3-32B MATH500 avg .798 vs. MCTS .758; AIME .311 vs. .278), and in some settings BG-MCTS merely ties or loses (e.g., Llama MATH500 10K ties Repeated Sampling), while the framing claims consistent superiority.

Comparability across baselines is weakened by heterogeneous node-generation units: 'Full' generation for some baselines and Sequential generation for others, with the authors arguing AB-MCTS-M's poor showing is a 'regime mismatch' rather than a methodological deficit. This makes it unclear how much of the advantage comes from the budget-aware policy versus these configuration choices.

Only a narrow slice of evaluation is used: MATH500 Level 5 only, and just 120 sampled UGPhysics questions, limiting the strength of generalization claims. Key hyperparameters (c=√2, κ=1, λ=1) are fixed by convention and the sensitivity sweep covers only one model/benchmark/budget combination with single runs.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is stated, and results depend on intricate pipeline details (reward-model prompt formatting, answer extraction regexes, prompt-based continuation 'But wait, let me think about the problem again.') that are difficult to replicate exactly from the manuscript alone.

The paper's own analysis (near-binary PRM scores, Table 10) reveals that the search signal is weak in this regime, which raises the question of how much of the improvement reflects principled budget-aware search versus incidental effects of the heuristic shaping; the manuscript acknowledges but does not resolve this.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly framed problem: existing tree-search decoding policies are budget-agnostic and treat the token budget merely as a stopping condition, which can cause late-stage over-branching or premature termination. The idea of conditioning selection and widening on the remaining budget ratio (ρ) is intuitive and cleanly instantiated in BG-PUCT (Eq. 3), the depth-biased completion term (Eq. 5), and the budget-guided widening trigger (Eq. 6).

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: three open-weight LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-32B), two math benchmarks (MATH500 Lv.5, AIME24/25), an additional physics benchmark (UGPhysics), and three budget levels, with most settings averaged over three trials. BG-MCTS achieves the best average accuracy in nearly all model/benchmark/budget combinations, which is consistent evidence for the central claim.

The analysis section goes beyond headline numbers: answer-reach rate curves (Figs. 3–5), depth–width trade-off analysis (Figs. 6a/6b, 12–13), answered-node precision statistics (Tables 4, 11), qualitative tree visualizations, and hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 6) all support the claimed wide-to-deep behavioral shift.

Reproducibility and fairness treatment is strong: prompts, answer extraction, LiteSearch budget-accounting subtleties (Appendix C), baseline hyperparameter search (Appendix B), PRM score saturation analysis (Appendix K), plus additional comparisons with beam search (Appendix I) and BG-MCTS with early stopping (Appendix J) are all documented.

Limitations are handled honestly, notably the discussion of GenPRM-7B score saturation (Sec. 6, Appendix K), the regime mismatch of AB-MCTS-M, and the coverage/quality trade-off for data synthesis (Appendix L).
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is a composition of fairly simple, ad hoc heuristics: multiplying the exploration bonus by ρ, adding a depth/d̂ans-shaped completion bias scaled by (1−ρ), and multiplying the widening score by ρ. There is no theoretical grounding for these specific functional forms (why linear annealing? why depth/d̂ans?), and the design choices (κ=1, λ=1, c=√2) appear to be defaults rather than principled choices.

The ablation results (Table 2) partially contradict the narrative that the three components are complementary: for Llama-3.1-8B, several ablated variants outperform the full method at specific budgets (e.g., Explore+Widen at 10K: .433 vs full .393; Explore+Exploit at 10K: .407 vs .393; Explore+Exploit at 30K: .433 vs .443 with Qwen at 10K dropping to .642 vs full .662). The claim 'Full BG-MCTS performs best overall' is only true on average, and Appendix H shows BG-MCTS without the generative node also beats full BG-MCTS at 10K (.679 vs .662). This variability weakens the attribution of gains to specific components.

No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported. On small benchmarks (AIME24/25 has 60 instances), differences of a few points at 10K budgets are within plausible run-to-run noise, and some individual budget cells show BG-MCTS merely tying baselines (e.g., MATH500/Llama 10K: .393 vs Repeated .393; AIME24 Qwen 10K: .156 vs MCTS .156).

Baseline strength is questionable in places: AB-MCTS-M performs dramatically worse than plain MCTS in the sequential setting (e.g., Llama MATH500 avg .171 vs .390), and the authors' explanation of an 'operating regime mismatch' is somewhat speculative; a stronger budget-aware baseline configuration would make the comparisons more convincing. Hyperparameter sensitivity is assessed only for BG-MCTS (one configuration per row, single run, one model/budget).

The Qwen3-32B setup disables its native reasoning mode, and the physics evaluation uses a substantially different rollout-based evaluator protocol, so generalization of the conclusions to modern reasoning-mode LLMs and to richer verifier signals (the setting where budget-awareness might matter most) remains untested.
